Exercise D.S9 — Hard: An invariant sublevel is a local guarantee
      
        For $\dot x=-x+x^3$, use $V=x^2$ to prove that every sublevel $V\le c$ with $0\lt c\lt1$ is forward invariant and converges to zero. Why does the same conclusion fail for $c=1$?
        Review if needed: this section and gradients and the chain rule.
        
          Show hint
          Inside the sublevel, $1-x^2\ge1-c\gt0$. Inspect the states $x=\pm1$.
        
        
          Show worked solution
          $\dot V=2x(-x+x^3)=-2x^2(1-x^2)$. On $V\le c$, this is at most $-2(1-c)V$.At the boundary $V=c$, the derivative is negative, so a trajectory cannot cross outward. The polynomial vector field is locally Lipschitz; remaining in this bounded sublevel also prevents finite escape. Comparison gives $V(t)\le V(0)e^{-2(1-c)t}$.At $c=1$, the boundary states $x=\pm1$ are equilibria and do not converge to zero. The closed sublevel remains invariant, but invariance alone does not prove attraction to the origin.
